statement: In eight unrelated children (five girls and three boys; three Native American, three Black and two White; aged 3 to 57 months when their development was tested) evaluated at a dysmorphology unit in Seattle and born to mothers who met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism (for more than 2 to 23 years, mean 9.4; delirium tremens in 5 of the 6 with a record, two of them in hospital with it during the pregnancy) and who drank heavily throughout pregnancy (no amounts recorded; none known to be dependent on another drug), a report that its authors call apparently the first to link a mother's alcoholism with abnormal development of the child's body (Jones et al., 1973; funded by US federal maternal and child health and National Institutes of Health grants and the National Foundation–March of Dimes; no conflict statement) describes a shared pattern: growth deficiency starting before birth in all eight (mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation, against a mean of 38 weeks; birth weights 1,550 to 2,500 g) with no catch-up later, even with adequate food during hospital stays for six of them or in foster care for three (after age 1, growth in length 65% and weight gain 38% of normal); short palpebral fissures (eye openings) in all eight; developmental delay in all eight (IQ or developmental index 57 to 83 in six and below 50 in one; none in the normal range, as the authors judged it); a small head in seven; an underdeveloped upper jaw in seven; altered palm creases in six; joint anomalies in five; heart anomalies in five (three of them murmurs that went away, taken to be septal defects that had closed); and folds of skin at the inner corner of the eye in four. The paper does not use the name fetal alcohol syndrome and refers to the pattern only as a syndrome; the two prevalence reviews read for this page date the first description of FAS to November 1973, one of them citing a later 1973 paper by two of the same authors with the name in its title, which was not read. This is a description of eight selected children, not a measure of how often the pattern follows heavy drinking in pregnancy or of what causes it: four children were recognised first and two more were found because they had the same features, possibly milder cases were left out on purpose, there was no comparison group and no count of children of mothers with alcoholism who were unaffected, the examiners knew the mothers' histories, the amount and timing of drinking were not recorded, smoking and other drug use were not reported, nutrition was only partly recorded, and poverty could not be separated out (all the families were on welfare); the authors nonetheless concluded that their data establish that maternal alcoholism can cause serious abnormal development before birth. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In 1973, a team in Seattle described eight young children, five girls and three boys, born to mothers who had had alcoholism for years and drank heavily all through pregnancy. All eight were small before and after birth and did not catch up, had short eye openings and were behind in development; seven had small heads, and many had a small upper jaw, unusual palm creases, joint problems or heart problems. The paper did not yet use the name fetal alcohol syndrome. It describes selected children: some were chosen because they had these signs, milder cases were left out, there was no comparison group, and the amount of drinking was not recorded. So it cannot show how often these signs follow heavy drinking in pregnancy, or what caused them.
population: Eight unrelated children (five girls, three boys; three Native American, three Black, two White) evaluated at the Dysmorphology Unit, Department of Pediatrics, University of Washington, Seattle, aged 3 to 57 months at developmental testing; four recognised first as sharing a pattern, two ascertained because they had its features and two because their mothers had chronic alcoholism
exposure: Born to mothers who met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism (2+ to 23 years, mean 9.4) and drank excessively throughout pregnancy, as the paper puts it; no amounts, beverages or timing recorded
comparator: None (no comparison group); measurements set against published norms for growth, head size, eye-opening length and development
outcome: Physical features (growth before and after birth, head size, eye openings, face, joints, palm creases, heart) and development (mental, motor and social), as present or absent in each child and as test scores
magnitude: Jones et al. 1973 (descriptive counts; no comparison group, no statistical tests). Table II, features present out of 8: developmental delay 8, microcephaly 7, prenatal growth deficiency 8, postnatal growth deficiency 8, short palpebral fissures 8, maxillary hypoplasia with relative prognathism 7, epicanthal folds 4, joint anomalies 5, altered palmar crease pattern 6, cardiac anomaly 5 (three presumed ventricular septal defects that closed). Table I: maternal alcoholism 7, 3, 4, 11, 2+, 10, 23 and 15 years (mean 9.4); delirium tremens 5 of 6 with data; maternal age at the birth 22 to 40 (mean 31.7); gestational age 34 to 44 weeks (mean 38); birth weight 1,550 to 2,500 g (mean 2,034); birth length 38 to 47 cm (mean 43.6); breech presentation 3 of 8. Growth: mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation; after 1 year of age, linear growth 65% and weight gain 38% of normal; mean daily weight gain 9 g against 26.6 g in upper-middle-class Seattle children and 24.4 g in high-risk children in a local programme; head circumference below the 3rd percentile at birth in 7 of 8 and at 1 year in 5 of 6 with data. Table III (age at testing 3 to 57 months): IQ or mental development index 59, 83, 75, 57, 79, 70 and below 50 (one child not scored); fine motor dysfunction in 5 of 6 tested; repetitive self-stimulating behaviour in 5.

evidence.locator: Clinical Findings › Methods of Patient Ascertainment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Eight children born to mothers with alcoholism were brought together and evaluated by the same two observers (K. J. and D. W. S.): four were recognised as having a similar pattern of altered growth and morphogenesis, two more were ascertained because they had the abnormal features found in the first four, and the remaining two because their mothers had chronic alcoholism. All the mothers met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism and drank excessively throughout the pregnancy; the mothers of patients 1 and 7 were in hospital with delirium tremens, patient 3 was born while her mother was in a stupor from drinking, and none of the mothers was known to be dependent on any other drug. No amounts of drinking are given.

Table I, patients 1 to 8: duration of maternal alcoholism 7, 3, 4, 11, 2+, 10, 23 and 15 years (mean 9.4); delirium tremens in 5 of 6 with data; maternal age at the birth 22 to 40 years (mean 31.7); gestational age 34 to 44 weeks (mean 38); birth weight 1550 to 2500 g (mean 2034); birth length 38 to 47 cm (mean 43.6); breech presentation 3 of 8.

Table II, features present out of 8: developmental delay 8, microcephaly 7, prenatal growth deficiency 8, postnatal growth deficiency 8, short palpebral fissures 8, maxillary hypoplasia with relative prognathism 7, epicanthal folds 4, joint anomalies 5, altered palmar crease pattern 6, cardiac anomaly 5. Patients 1 to 3 are Native American (American Indian), 4 to 6 Black, and 7 and 8 White. The case reports describe five girls (patients 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7) and three boys (patients 5, 6 and 8).

All eight had prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency: with a mean gestational age of 38 weeks, mean birth length and weight were at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation. None showed catch-up growth, neither during hospital admissions for failure to thrive in six children, with adequate caloric intake recorded, nor in foster care in three. After 1 year of age, average linear growth was 65% and weight gain 38% of normal; mean daily weight gain was 9 g, against 26.6 g in upper-middle-class Seattle children and 24.4 g in high-risk children in a local maternal and infant care programme. Head circumference was below the 3rd percentile for gestational age at birth in seven of the eight, and by 1 year below the 3rd percentile for height age and for chronological age in five of the six with data.

evidence.locator: Clinical Findings › Performance, 1st paragraph (p. 1269, continuing on p. 1270); Table III (p. 1270)
evidence.extracted: Performance testing was done by one psychologist (A. P. S.) for all but patient 5. Table III, patients 1 to 8: age at testing 14, 3, 57, 46, 18, 40, 48 and 34 months; IQ or mental development index 59, 83, 75, 57, not given, 79, 70 and below 50. None of the children performed within the normal range, and social and motor performance matched mental age more than chronological age; fine motor dysfunction was present in five of the six tested, and repetitive self-stimulating behaviour such as head rolling, head banging or rocking in five.

The authors interpret the short palpebral fissures as secondary to deficient growth of the eyes (microphthalmia noted at birth in patients 1 and 7), the maxillary hypoplasia as producing relative prognathism, and the joint and palmar-crease changes as consequences of limited movement or aberrant position early in fetal life; of the five children with a cardiac anomaly, three were considered to have had a ventricular septal defect that closed before 1 year of age. The paragraph calls the pattern this syndrome; the paper nowhere uses the name fetal alcohol syndrome.

The summary describes eight unrelated children of three ethnic groups, born to mothers with chronic alcoholism, with a similar pattern of craniofacial, limb and cardiovascular defects, prenatal-onset growth deficiency and developmental delay, and calls this apparently the first reported association between maternal alcoholism and abnormal morphogenesis in the offspring.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 1270), 3rd paragraph (p. 1270, continuing on p. 1271) and 4th paragraph (p. 1271)
evidence.extracted: The authors take the similar pattern to suggest a single cause, most likely an effect of the maternal alcoholism, with direct ethanol toxicity the most obvious possibility, and name acetaldehyde, an unknown agent in the beverages, or general or specific maternal undernutrition as alternatives; they argue against undernutrition because the pattern had not been recognised in children of undernourished women without alcoholism and because length was more affected than weight. All the families were living on welfare, with parents' education from eighth grade to college; the children in foster care (patient 1 from birth, patient 3 from age 2 to 4) did not perform better, and the authors state that it is difficult to determine how far the socioeconomic situation or continued maternal alcoholism affected development.

Two of the children have partially affected siblings who were also born while their mothers had alcoholism; other siblings are said to be normal, some born before and some after their mothers' alcoholism began. The authors set out the pattern in the more severely affected children, purposely leave out possible mildly affected cases, and conclude that their data are enough to show that a mother's alcoholism can cause serious abnormal development before birth.
evidence.quote: the data are sufficient to establish that maternal alcoholism can cause serious aberrant fetal development

evidence.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 2nd paragraph; reference 13
evidence.extracted: Popova et al. state that FAS was first described in 1973, citing Jones and Smith, Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy (Lancet 1973; 302: 999–1001), and begin their FAS search on 1 November 1973, when, they write, FAS was first described. Editors' note: the paper read here (Jones et al., Lancet 1973; 301: 1267–1271, 9 June 1973) is the earlier report by the same group and does not use the name.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_jones_1973 overall high (editors' domains; no standard instrument fits a case series): two children were ascertained because they had the features and possibly milder cases were left out, so the uniformity of the pattern is partly built in; the examiners knew the mothers' histories and had already recognised the pattern; norms were not matched to sex or ethnicity (head size against norms for boys for five girls, eye openings against a mean for White children for six Native American or Black children); three of the five heart anomalies are presumed from murmurs that went away. Counted once.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: what was described in these eight children. As a description of the syndrome in general it would be indirect (the most severely affected children, mothers with long-standing alcoholism), which the statement says.

imprecision.note: Eight children: counts such as 5 of 8 fit a wide range of proportions.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a single historical report.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim from a case series: it starts low (METHODS §6.3) and is never upgraded; risk of bias and imprecision each take a level, so very low. Status single study: no other description of the pattern was read; the later 1973 paper that the two prevalence reviews cite as the first description of FAS (Jones and Smith) was not read. The claim is cited for what was described and in whom, never for how often heavy drinking in pregnancy leads to the pattern, for any amount of drinking, or for its cause: the authors' conclusion that maternal alcoholism can cause serious abnormal fetal development goes beyond what eight selected children without a comparison group can show. That this was the first such report is the authors' own statement and was not checked against earlier literature. Every number from the scanned PDF was checked on the rendered pages; Tables I to III have no text layer.
